A cash runway is defined as the length of time it would take a company to run out of money if it kept spending at its current rate of cash burn. data.title: Will Bonterra Resources (CVE:BTR) Spend Its Cash Wisely?
data.description:
We can readily understand why investors are attracted to unprofitable companies. For example, although Amazon.com made losses for many years after listing, if you had bought and held the shares since 1999, you would have made a fortune. Having said that, unprofitable companies are risky because they could potentially burn through all their cash and become distressed.

So should Bonterra Resources (CVE:BTR) shareholders be worried about its cash burn? In this report, we will consider the company's annual negative free cash flow, henceforth referring to it as the 'cash burn'. First, we'll determine its cash runway by comparing its cash burn with its cash reserves.

This technology could replace computers: discover the 20 stocks are working to make quantum computing a reality.

When Might Bonterra Resources Run Out Of Money?

A company's cash runway is the amount of time it would take to burn through its cash reserves at its current cash burn rate. As at September 2026, Bonterra Resources had cash of CA$15m and no debt. Looking at the last year, the company burnt through CA$13m. So it had a cash runway of approximately 14 months from September 2026. While that cash runway isn't too concerning, sensible holders would be peering into the distance, and considering what happens if the company runs out of cash. The image below shows how its cash balance has been changing over the last few years.

View our latest analysis for Bonterra Resources

How Is Bonterra Resources' Cash Burn Changing Over Time?

Because Bonterra Resources isn't currently generating revenue, we consider it an early-stage business. So while we can't look to sales to understand growth, we can look at how the cash burn is changing to understand how expenditure is trending over time. Over the last year its cash burn actually increased by a very significant 89%. While this spending increase is no doubt intended to drive growth, if the trend continues the company's cash runway will shrink very quickly. Bonterra Resources makes us a little nervous due to its lack of substantial operating revenue. We prefer most of the stocks on this list of stocks that analysts expect to grow.

Can Bonterra Resources Raise More Cash Easily?

While Bonterra Resources does have a solid cash runway, its cash burn trajectory may have some shareholders thinking ahead to when the company may need to raise more cash. Issuing new shares, or taking on debt, are the most common ways for a listed company to raise more money for its business. Many companies end up issuing new shares to fund future growth. We can compare a company's cash burn to its market capitalisation to get a sense for how many new shares a company would have to issue to fund one year's operations.

Bonterra Resources has a market capitalisation of CA$46m and burnt through CA$13m last year, which is 28% of the company's market value. That's fairly notable cash burn, so if the company had to sell shares to cover the cost of another year's operations, shareholders would suffer some costly dilution.

Is Bonterra Resources' Cash Burn A Worry?

Even though its increasing cash burn makes us a little nervous, we are compelled to mention that we thought Bonterra Resources' cash runway was relatively promising. Summing up, we think the Bonterra Resources' cash burn is a risk, based on the factors we mentioned in this article. data.title: What Investors Got Wrong About Applied Digital Before The Drop
data.description:

The Two Applied Digital Stories Investors Had To Weigh

The shares cost US$21.37 at the start, and anyone looking at Applied Digital then was really choosing between two tight but very different stories.

The bullish narrative saw Fair Value at US$24, or 12% above the start price. That view leaned on assumed revenue growth of 82.0% a year over three years and profit margins shifting from heavy losses to 28.7%, supported by long AI leases.

The bearish case put Fair Value at US$13, or 39% below the start price. It accepted fast 75.4% revenue growth assumptions but focused on high debt and the risk that tighter regulation and supply chain problems would squeeze margins to just 2.6% and justify a 273.2x future P/E.

What The Evidence Did To The Applied Digital Story

Applied Digital signed several 15 year AI leases worth tens of billions of US dollars in contracted revenue, which directly backed the bullish focus on long contracts and hyperscaler demand. The measured results told a different story on profitability. Revenue reached US$341.9m in Q1 2027, while the business still reported a loss and net margin fell to -64.7%. The period cut both ways.

The whole episode turned on one assumption. You can accept aggressive growth forecasts only if you also track whether profit and net margin are actually moving toward the promised target, quarter by quarter, not just whether big contracts are announced.

What You Are Paying For In Applied Digital Today

Applied Digital trades at US$11.49 today after a 45.5% loss over the past year, and the bearish analyst Narrative on Simply Wall St places its Fair Value above that level based on contracted AI and HPC growth.

The same Narrative argues that for the higher figure to hold, new AI and power projects would need funding on terms that keep interest costs from overwhelming future earnings.

"Although Applied Digital highlights roughly $36 billion of contracted revenue across long term leases, the recent net loss of about $221 million from continuing operations in fiscal Q1 2027, driven by very high SG&A and noncash warrant losses, signals that scaling into this contract base could still leave the company struggling to translate future revenue into sustained earnings and cash flow."

data.title: Is Honeywell International (HON) Cheaper After A 46% Slide?
data.description:
Honeywell International has seen its share price fall sharply year to date, and that slide puts a fresh spotlight on whether the cash the business can generate really lines up with where the stock now trades. With a Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) estimate available, investors are increasingly focused on how Honeywell's current price stacks up against the long term cash flows its operations may support.

  • The stock is down 45.7% year to date, which puts the recent selloff front and center for anyone asking if the move reflects a reset in expectations for Honeywell's future cash generation.
  • Recent updates on automation, physical AI and smart building platforms, along with a reported backlog of nearly US$19b, may support views on the durability and timing of Honeywell's cash inflows from these growth areas.
  • What if you looked at Honeywell International through its earnings instead? See why Honeywell International's 7.5x P/E tells a different valuation story.

The issue now is whether Honeywell's current share price is justified by the cash flows implied by its intrinsic value estimate under the Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) approach.

If you want a yardstick for Honeywell International's AI driven automation and cash flow story, compare it with the 53 AI infrastructure stocks.

Does Honeywell International Look Pricey on Cash Flow?

The Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model here projects what Honeywell International might generate for shareholders based on its future free cash generation. Latest twelve month free cash flow sits around $935.1m, while analyst and model estimates point to Free Cash Flow to Equity moving into the low $3b range over the next decade, then easing into slower growth. That pattern reflects a mature industrial and automation group where cash generation is expected to be sizeable but not racing higher every year.

The DCF outcome indicates Honeywell's implied intrinsic value is meaningfully below the current share price of $212.64, so the market is attaching a richer tag to the stock than the cash flow stream here would support on its own. Recent emphasis on pure play automation, physical AI and data center infrastructure, backed by a backlog near $19b, helps explain why investors may be willing to pay up despite a more measured long term cash flow glide path in the model. The Honeywell International Narrative: What Would Justify Today's Price?

Honeywell International's Simply Wall St Narratives pick up where the DCF puzzle leaves off by spelling out which paths for revenue, profitability and earnings would need to play out for the stock to be worth meaningfully more or less than today’s price on the Community page. Each narrative links its valuation figure to a specific view on how Honeywell International's growth, margins and risks could evolve, giving you a reference point you can revisit as fresh information arrives.

Optimists see Honeywell International as an automation and AI infrastructure play that the market is underrating, while skeptics think expectations already bake in most of the upside.

Bull case: 34% undervalued

According to niteco, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community, the opportunity sits in how the post spin automation story is being framed.

“Everyone is buying the power generators and the semiconductors, nobody has priced what happens when $19 billion of building, industrial, and energy technology backlog gets re-rated as a pure-play AI infrastructure and energy transition play…”

Bear case: roughly fairly valued

The bearish analyst Narrative on Simply Wall St argues that Honeywell already trades as if the automation shift goes mostly to plan.

“The current figures for organic growth, margin expansion, and earnings guidance suggest a share price that already reflects Honeywell International as a fairly valued pure-play automation company, with execution risk if high-growth and margin targets are not met…”
